transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-12-01
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 60 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Carlos Mendez (Redwood CSM), Michael Chen (CISO, Stratus), Aisha Roberts (Infra Lead, Stratus), Daniel Kim (Security Architect, Stratus), Lena Park (Compliance Manager, Stratus)

Auto-generated summary (may be imperfect): Deep dive on private VPC pattern, need for strict egress controls and KMS integration; customer wants SOC 2 artifacts, RBAC/SSO details, and an ops runbook for on-prem option.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Jordan from Redwood, AE on the account. With me is Priya, our security / infra SE, and Carlos from CS.
[00:10] Michael Chen: Great thanks, Jordan. On our side Michael Chen, CISO, and Aisha and Daniel and Lena. We wanted to focus on the private VPC option, specifically how you handle network isolation and egress.
[00:22] Jordan Lee: Perfect. Priya, do you want to kick off with the high-level architecture?
[00:25] Priya Nair: Sure, thanks. So Redwood Private runs a customer-dedicated control plane and can be deployed in a couple ways — VPC-hosted on the customer's cloud account or on-prem package. The common pattern is we create dedicated subnets for the serving tier, a management/control plane subnet, and a bastion or jump-box for maintenance. All infra talk: we prefer separate AZs for redundancy but that's optional.
[00:46] Aisha Roberts: On the VPC-hosted model, are we giving Redwood accounts any inbound access or is it fully customer-managed?
[00:52] Priya Nair: It's customer-managed. The control plane is optionally customer-controlled; in the VPC model Redwood provides deployable templates (CloudFormation/Terraform) but the customer keeps the keys and the VPC. For hosted-managed private, we use a private peering or transit gateway but that's usually for Dedicated customers. There's no open inbound from the public internet to the serving tier unless you explicitly configure a public ALB.
[01:18] Daniel Kim: And egress? Our security policy is strict: only certain destinations allowed and we need to block everything else. How do you support allowlists?
[01:26] Priya Nair: We recommend using egress NAT with very specific routing rules and Security Group or NACL rules to restrict outbound IPs. For service endpoints — like model artifact pulls or image registries — we support VPC endpoints (S3, ECR) and you can route through a proxy appliance. For third-party telemetry or metrics, we provide an option to route that via your telemetry VPC and tokenized TLS.
[01:46] Michael Chen: Is there any persistent egress to Redwood-hosted endpoints for telemetry or health checks? We've seen other vendors phone-home and that's a blocker.
[01:54] Jordan Lee: Good question. For the Private VPC deploy we can run in a completely offline mode — no outbound to Redwood — if you choose on-prem, it's air-gapped. The standard VPC deploy can be configured with zero outbound except for approved services. The only time Redwood endpoints are contacted is if you want us to manage upgrades or collect aggregated telemetry; otherwise those are optional and we document the endpoints and ports.
[02:20] Lena Park: From a compliance angle, we need audit logs retained for seven years and immutable. What does Redwood provide?
[02:28] Priya Nair: We emit audit logs for admin actions, API access, and model rollouts. In the VPC model logs can be pushed to your own S3 or object store and we recommend enabling server-side encryption with your KMS. For immutability, we recommend a WORM bucket policy or S3 Object Lock. We can also stream logs to your SIEM via Kinesis or Pub/Sub equivalents.
[02:49] Michael Chen: Okay. And do you support integration with our KMS (customer-managed keys) for encrypting model data at rest and in transit?
[02:56] Priya Nair: Yes. We support customer-managed keys for disk and object encryption. For secrets and keys we integrate with customer KMS/HSM providers — AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, Google KMS, and on-prem HSMs through PKCS#11. There's an initial key rotation handshake during setup and we support rotating keys without full redeploy.
[03:16] Daniel Kim: How do you handle ephemeral disk and KV cache encryption? We want both at-rest and in-use protections.
[03:23] Priya Nair: Ephemeral disks are encrypted with the host disk encryption using your key. The KV cache lives in memory and is backed to encrypted storage — the in-use memory is not encrypted by default (hardware enclaves not in scope for standard private) but we've got mitigations: process isolation, minimal access, and options to wipe KV on restart. For extremely high threat models we can discuss SGX/SEV-based enclaves as a paid engagement.
[03:47] Aisha Roberts: For SSO and RBAC, does Redwood support SAML and SCIM for provisioning roles? We need fine-grained RBAC mapped to AD groups.
[03:56] Priya Nair: Yes, SAML SSO is supported for Console access and SCIM for user provisioning. RBAC is role-based with custom role mapping to your AD groups; we can mirror groups and sync via SCIM. For API keys we recommend per-service accounts with limited scopes and short TTLs; Redwoods supports token rotation.
[04:16] Michael Chen: SOC 2 evidence — can you send us the Type II report and the list of controls mapped to our internal requirements?
[04:23] Jordan Lee: Absolutely. I'll share the SOC 2 Type II report, the ISO 27001 summary, and our control mapping doc. We'll redact customer-unique info as appropriate.
[04:31] Lena Park: Are penetration test reports available?
[04:34] Jordan Lee: We have summary pen test results and an attestation; full reports are available under NDA.
[04:40] Daniel Kim: One of our engineers asked about firewalling between model-serving nodes and the orchestration plane. Is there mutual TLS between components?
[04:48] Priya Nair: All internal services use mutual TLS. We also strongly recommend service-level policies — network policies via security groups and microsegmentation for the serving tier. Port exposure is minimal, usually just the TLS serving port and the metrics/health port restricted to the management subnet.
[05:05] Aisha Roberts: For egress allowlist, can you give an example of the minimal set of destinations? We need to update our change control docs.
[05:12] Priya Nair: Yes — typical list includes internal artifact stores (S3/ECR with VPC endpoints), your container registry, STS endpoints for KMS, OS package mirrors if you allow OS updates, and optional telemetry endpoints. We'll provide a canonical list in the VPC template.
[05:28] Michael Chen: On data residency, we need to ensure model prompts and customer data never leave our chosen region. Is that enforceable?
[05:36] Priya Nair: Yes — you can pin the region for both control plane and serving. For hybrid we can ensure the serving tier stays in-region; any backups or artifact stores can be restricted similarly. We support customer-specified object store endpoints so things never cross borders.
[05:51] Jordan Lee: Quick note — some customers use a Dedicated deployment instead if they want Redwood-managed infra but single-tenant GPU pools. That still supports the same RBAC/KMS patterns and private networking.
[06:03] Daniel Kim: What about egress from model execution — like external API calls from a model plugin or tool?
[06:10] Priya Nair: Model tooling that makes outbound calls runs in a sandbox and outbound is blocked by default. If you need controlled external calls we recommend a proxy service in your VPC with strict allowlist. We can also provide a webhook relay that validates and signs requests.
[06:27] Michael Chen: For logging retention, is there a TTL we can configure per log type?
[06:32] Priya Nair: Yes, retention policies are configurable. Audit logs, metrics, and raw transcripts can have independent retention and can be exported to your storage for long-term retention.
[06:41] Lena Park: Are there any known gaps for SOC2 or ISO alignment with Private deployments?
[06:46] Jordan Lee: The Private deployment basically pushes many controls to the customer boundary — so the gap is the customer's responsibility to configure the VPC, logging, and retention policies. Redwood provides the control evidence for the software and managed services we operate. We'll provide a mapping doc showing which controls are customer-responsibility vs Redwood responsibility.
[07:03] Aisha Roberts: On firewalling specifics — do you recommend NACLs or SGs as the primary control?
[07:08] Priya Nair: Security Groups for per-instance controls and NACLs for subnet-level defense in depth. Also recommend host-based firewalling on the bastion and strict route tables to control egress.
[07:20] Daniel Kim: For the bench tests, we want to validate that egress is fully blocked except allowed IPs and that metrics forwarding doesn't leak data. What telemetry options are available?
[07:29] Carlos Mendez: We can run a bench with our infra engineers and run a simulated workload while capturing egress attempts. We'll provide a checklist for what to watch for and a test plan.
[07:37] Jordan Lee: Great — let's capture action items. Everyone, please confirm due dates in the next 24 hours.
[07:43] Michael Chen: Quick follow up — for on-prem installs, what's the expected timeline for a POC?
[07:48] Priya Nair: For on-prem it's 6-8 weeks for a minimal POC assuming hardware is available; VPC-hosted private can be done in 2-3 weeks. We'll provide an onboarding runbook.
[07:58] Lena Park: Any additional compliance artifacts for data residency?
[08:02] Jordan Lee: We'll include region-specific attestations and our data handling policy.
[08:06] Aisha Roberts: For the network diagram you send, can you include example security group rules and NACL entries?
[08:12] Priya Nair: Yep, that's part of the VPC template pack.
[08:15] Daniel Kim: One last thing — do you support ephemeral workloads wiping on shutdown? We need assurance that model prompts are not retained beyond processing window.
[08:23] Priya Nair: Ephemeral logs and caches are wiped on shutdown by default; we also support disabling transcript persistence and not storing prompts unless explicitly enabled. We'll note this in the control doc.
[08:34] Jordan Lee: OK wrapping up. Quick recap of next steps: we'll share SOC 2/ISO docs, VPC template, and schedule bench for early December. Redwood to provide pricing estimate for Dedicated + Private. Stratus to share firewall rules, preferred region, and confirm bench attendees.
[08:52] Michael Chen: Sounds good, thanks everyone.
[08:55] Jordan Lee: Thanks all, we'll follow up via email with the artifacts and calendar invite for the bench.

End of transcript.
